result.weather: A front has moved through: wind speed and direction over the hotspots differ from calibration. Drag, shear, veer and updraft are unchanged. Use measure_wind.

notes.text: I'm starting by reading through the mission briefing to get oriented.

I'm working out which parameters need calibration: drag, shear, veer, and updraft. Wind readings at aircraft altitude, taken during operation at several heights, can give the wind profile directly, so the calibration effort mostly goes to drag and updraft. I'm also noting that shear and veer can be estimated from the noisy wind readings themselves, about 20 of them with 0.5 m/s and 4 degree noise. Now I'm starting to sketch the plan for the test drops.

I'm settling on test drops away from the smoke at 30, 90 and 150 m to pin down drag and the wind profile, with a few through the smoke column for updraft. I'm also noting that drag sets the fall speed, so it matters a lot for where each load lands.

I'm checking the wind speed at each height, and the veer works out to about -27.5 degrees per 100 m, putting the direction at 100 m near 35 degrees. Now I'm taking the log of the speed ratio to get the shear exponent.

I'm working out the speed fit, getting about 0.3 for the shear exponent and roughly 6.0 m/s at 100 m. Next I'm turning to the drag problem, using the 150 m fall time to see how much drag matters and trying a few drag values.

The fall times came out too long, so the drag is probably set too high. The along-track distances are also running short: about 18 m off for tests 1 and 2 heading north, and 23 m off for test 3 heading east. I'll lower the drag and try 0.03.

Still running short along the track, so I'm considering a slightly lower drag coefficient, around 0.027 or perhaps 0.026. The test 2 drop from 30 m, with its 3.3 s fall, shows a -6.2 offset with essentially zero time difference, which points to along-track sensitivity to drag at low altitude. Its crosswind offset of 0.2 looks fine, so I'll try 0.026 next.

I'm sorting through the drag estimate of about 0.027 and the three test displacements, which point in different directions, so the wind is likely mixing their effects. Test 3 heads east at 90 m, and the wind looks to be coming from roughly 37 degrees, so I'll leave the fine-tuning for later, since wind and shear will be measured again in operation anyway.

Now I'm considering the updraft through the smoke column, which could slow the fall and stretch the drift. With a terminal speed around 19 m/s, I want the load to fall nearly vertically inside the column, so I'll release it high and upstream so it lands near the center, and I'll simulate that aim before I commit.

I'm checking that a release from (-68,-100) on heading 35 roughly lands near the center when there's no updraft, and that an updraft makes the fall longer and pushes it further downwind. I'm planning two updraft drops to test sensitivity: one at 150 m on heading 35 from that point, and one on a different geometry, heading 215 into the wind from (68,100).

I'm now weighing whether a heading-into-the-wind drop would land short. I'll run the first updraft drop, compare it to the no-updraft case to estimate the effect, and only then decide on a second, differently placed drop.

The test 5 landing point at (43.8, 66.1) is outside the smoke, so it didn't drift much at all. Released from (55, 80) at 45 m/s, that's only about 18 m, which seems odd, since with no wind it should have gone roughly 110 m. A 6 m/s headwind over 9.6 s might cut maybe 50 m, but that still doesn't account for such a short distance, so I'm wondering whether I've misread something.

I'm checking whether the drag-relative-to-air explanation could account for the short landing distance, since the projectile's speed against the air would be lower than 45 m/s. Then I'll compare against test 4, where the fall time stretched from 9.64 s to 11.33 s once the updraft was included, which suggests the updraft had a large effect.
Test 5 checks out, so the physics model holds up. Test 4 shows a negative dt of -0.34, which means the updraft needs to be stronger, so I'll try an updraft of 7.

I'm working through a nonlinear interpolation from 5 to 7, estimating the updraft at about 5.82 from the linear fit, though the position at 5 already shows a y-offset of 2.3. That residual hints at a lower updraft or a wind error, so I'm comparing the position changes at both points to estimate the slope per unit.

I'm checking the position residual against the time-based estimate, which conflicts and may point to off wind or drag parameters. I'm planning a few more test drops at different altitudes and headings to constrain the drag and wind before refining the fit.

I'm weighing whether to run a test drop at about 100 m altitude with a 45 m/s speed and a 125° heading, using the earlier drop at 90 m as a rough guide to how far the load travels.

I'm aiming for a landing near the origin, so I'm shifting the release point by about (-18.7, -5.9) to (-78.7, 14.1), accepting that the updraft makes this only approximate. I'll also plan a non-smoke drop at 120 m heading 270 at speed 80 from (0, -300), plus a low-altitude smoke drop at 50 m, starting with test 6 and the non-smoke drop.

I'm going through the wind readings at each point, then averaging them and working out the veer from 30 to 150, which comes to about -24 per 100, so the direction at 100 lands near 37.

I'm checking the 90 and 120 points against the fitted line, where the residuals look noisy. Then I'm running a linear regression of direction on height, which gives a veer of about -24.8 and a direction near 36.8 at 100. Next I'm setting up the log regression for speed.

I'm working out the log regression for speed, summing the cross-products of the centered log values, and starting on the sum of squares for the x terms.

I'm finishing the slope calculation for the speed regression, which comes out to about 0.22 with an intercept giving a wind speed near 5.84. That gives a working hypothesis of roughly 5.85 for speed, 37 for direction, a shear of 0.22, and a veer of -25, which I'll compare against the drag and updraft values.

The x-errors are all positive, so the predictions keep landing too far east. Test 7 suggests drag is too high, but test 3 suggests drag is too low, so the conflict probably points to the wind's east component being overestimated.

I'm weighing whether the north wind component is too weak, since tests 1 and 2 fell short northward while test 5 overshot southward. Rotating the wind direction toward north would shift some of the east component into north, which could explain the pattern, though test 2's short northward miss looks too large to come from wind alone.

I'm checking whether the systematic eastward bias and the residuals that are roughly within noise point to the same fix. A mean miss of about 2.1 m is close to what the 1.5 m noise alone would produce, but the consistent positive dx across all seven tests still looks real. I'll try shifting the wind direction to 33 degrees to see whether that helps.

I'm finding the sensitivity is large, about 3.5 m of x-shift over 5° on long falls, so I've overshot. Per degree, the first test gave roughly -0.7 in x and +0.48 in y, and all the y values now look positive. I'm trying a direction near 35 with slightly lower speed, and I'm checking the means at 32 and 37 to see where it lands.

I'm checking the drag and updraft values against the calibration falls, since fall time mostly depends on drag and the residuals sit near zero for the non-smoke tests. The drag of about 0.027 looks good to within ±0.0005, and the updraft from the smoke tests comes out around 5.9 to 6 m/s, so I'll use 35 and an updraft of 6 for the next check.

With three test drops left, I'm weighing which would be most useful. The operation will cover different wind, hotspot intensity and altitude ranges, possibly low altitudes at high speed, where drag uncertainty hits along-track range hardest. I'm thinking about using the remaining drops to pin down drag and updraft further, starting with a fast low drop.

I'm settling on three follow-up drops: a fast, low-altitude non-smoke run to tighten the along-track drag estimate, then two smoke drops to probe the updraft, one at mid altitude on the opposite crosswind heading and one lower down. I'm also noting that the extra wind readings near 60 m will help with the shear and veer picture.

I'm working through the release points for tests 9 and 10. For test 9 the landing was at (47.3, 9.6) from (80, -60), so the shift is (-47.3, -9.6) and the release becomes (32.7, -69.6). Landing near the center may change how the updraft acts, since the glider spends more time in the column, but I'll take that as fine for now. Test 10 shifts by (-12.7, -0.6), giving a release of (-12.7, -75.6). Test 8 was the non-smoke run, which came out fast and low.
I'm comparing the options now.

I'm checking whether the updraft would be stronger here: the predicted position is too far east, which means the aircraft didn't drift far enough along its northwest heading. Projecting the residual onto the track and cross-track directions gives roughly 3.4 m short along track and 2.6 m off to the side. Next I'm looking at the southward heading run at 80 m/s.

I'm testing whether a weaker drag value fits better, since most residuals point to drag running a bit high, though lowering it would shorten the fall times, which are already close to zero error. I'm also re-fitting the wind and updraft values against all ten points to see whether the new low-altitude readings change the picture.

Now I'm recomputing the regression over all ten points, working through the mean altitude and mean direction first. Next I'm summing the cross-products of the deviations, which comes to a negative total.

I'm finishing the regression on the wind data: the altitude-and-direction sums give a veer of about -20.8 per meter, putting the direction at 100 m near 35.4. Next I'm working out the speed log values for each point and starting the mean of those.

I'm finishing the regression's cross-products: the deviation products sum to about 0.583. Next I'm computing the sum of squares for the speed-log values.

I'm finishing the sum of squares, which comes to 2.663, so the slope is about 0.219. Working the intercept back to zero altitude gives roughly 5.85 m/s. That leaves shear at 0.22, veer at -21, wind speed at 5.85, and direction at 35.4. I'll try a drag of 0.0265 and an updraft of 6.2 with these values.

Test 8's dt of -0.15 is still there while test 4 shows 0, which is odd. I'm checking whether test 8 ran through the column, then working out the mean dx from the ten values, which comes to 0.93. Next I'm doing the same averaging for dy.

The bias from those averages points to the wind being a bit too strong in the northeast direction. I'm going to test a slightly lower wind speed, around 5.6, and see whether the drift lines up better.

Sensitivity is high: a 0.25 m/s error becomes roughly 1-2 m on long drops, but averaging about 15 readings with 0.5 m/s noise each brings it down to around 0.13-0.2 m/s, which is acceptable. Tests 1 and 5 (both at 150 m) show negative residuals, while test 10 (60 m, fast) is positive. Test 5, heading 215 into the wind, is off by -3.3 m in y and -2.4 m in x, so the prediction lands too far south.

I'm checking whether shifting the shear exponent to around 0.3 would fit the residual pattern: test 1 needs more northward wind, and test 10 needs less wind at low altitude. I'll try a shear of 0.32 with a surface wind of 5.7.

The noise is about 1.5 per axis, so the two persistent offsets for tests 5 and 2 are only around 1.5σ and sit close to the noise floor. I don't want to over-fit the sum of squares. What matters for operation is drag, updraft, shear and veer, and the ±0.1 shear uncertainty matters moderately, so wind readings at several altitudes should help pin it down.

The test 8 residual stands out at -0.16, with the predicted fall shorter than observed, which points to more updraft there. Tests 4, 9 and 6 sit near zero or slightly off, so I'm considering nudging updraft up to about 6.4, maybe 6.5, and checking whether that leaves test 4 out of balance.

I'm settling the updraft at about 6.35, which sits between the 6.3 and 6.4 results. The non-smoke time differences run slightly negative, so I'm nudging drag up to roughly 0.0267. Next I'm checking the position residuals on tests 4 and 8, since they seem to push the predictions in a consistent direction.

I'm checking the test 8 heading residual as well, which reads as undershooting along the track but looks like noise. I'm locking in the final calibration: drag at 0.0267, shear around 0.3, veer near -21, and updraft at 6.35.

I'm planning wind measurements at five altitudes, about 58, 103, 117, 122 and 133 metres. The idea is to take readings near 100 m and a few at 50 and 150 m to check the profile, then convert them to 100 m values using the known shear and veer. I'm considering four readings at each altitude, which would come to twenty.

I'm weighing whether to use the remaining readings for fitting rather than spreading them evenly. A tentative plan is to start with ten readings: three at 60 m, two at 100 m, three at 120 m and two at 135 m.

I'm noticing the noise is sometimes bigger than 0.5, so I'll take more readings. Next I'm converting the 58 m reading to 100 m equivalents, working out the speed factor and the direction correction from the shear and veer.

Now I'm checking the corrected readings at 103, 120 and 133 metres, applying the speed factor and the direction shift to each. The averages come out near 6.39 for speed and 61.4 degrees for direction. A rough veer check from the profile is in the right range, and I'm working out the shear exponent from the speed ratio.

The shear exponent checks out at about 0.28, close to the 0.3 I assumed. I'll take ten more readings at the drop altitudes to tighten the average.

I'm converting the next set of values, recalculating the figures for entries 58, 103, 117, and 122 with their decay factors and directional adjustments.

I'm rechecking the remaining adjusted speeds and directions, then comparing the averaged raw groups to see how the heading drifts from the 58 group to the 133 group.

Now I'm checking the speed profile against the raw readings: the shear works out to about 0.31 from the 58 m group to the 133 m group, which agrees with the 0.3–0.32 range. I'm settling the veer near -21, with -20 as a possible alternative.

I'm checking the calibration fit against the shear of 0.32: the converted readings come out near 5.91 at the geometric mean, a bit above the fitted 5.7, so the instrument values may sit about 3.5% higher than the fit implies, possibly just noise.

I'm settling on a compromise wind speed of about 6.38, since the calibration mean runs slightly high but is within noise. The direction from calibration matches the fit closely enough to leave alone. For each drop I'm weighing heading, altitude, and speed, and leaning toward the lowest altitude in range to shorten the fall and reduce wind sensitivity.

Now I'm working out the release point for the first target at (466, 1076): I'll simulate a drop from there, take the impact offset, and then shift the release by that offset. After that I'll re-run the simulation to check it, since the updraft depends on where the release sits relative to the fire.

I'm planning to simulate a release from the first target at (466, 1076), with all five targets run in parallel, to get each impact offset before shifting the release points.

I'm working through the release offsets for each trial, noting where the plume lands given the early-fall updraft, and the sequence of corrected release positions is coming together.

I'm checking the last trial's corrected release position, (-1034.9, 31.2), and then I'll run the simulation on all five.

I'm going through the per-target errors now. For T1 and T2 the corrections are moderate, and T3 shows a bigger plume effect, so I'm considering iterating with damping. T4 is already good enough, and I'm checking T5's error.

I'm re-running the simulation for T1, T2, T3 and T5 to get updated corrections for those targets.

I'm checking the T3 and T5 corrections: the ratio from the earlier shifts puts the T3 release near (1140.2, -951.0) and the T5 release near (-1040.5, 30.9).

The release points for T3 and T5 are small corrections, and I'm going to refine them since the calculations are cheap. I'm also weighing whether to check how sensitive the result is to the altitude and speed choices, and whether the wind correction should use 6.4 or 6.44, though that difference is minor.

Now I'm executing the drops for T1 through T5, each with its heading, altitude, speed, and position.

Now I'm finishing the coordinates for T5.
